opus-5.5.text:
I think it shapes it much more than people realize. When you sit down to design that spreadsheet, before you run anything, you're forced to decide what the columns are. What are the variables you care about? What's the baseline? What counts as a result? That act of laying it out is basically formulating your hypothesis space. If you can't figure out what the columns should be, it usually means you don't yet understand what question you're asking.

I tell my students this a lot: the spreadsheet is a kind of thinking tool, not just bookkeeping. A good one tells a story. You look at a row and you know exactly what changed relative to the row above it, and why you ran it. A bad one is just a pile of numbers, a hundred runs with random hyperparameters, and three months later nobody, including yourself, can say what you learned.

It also enforces a certain discipline about controlled experiments. In deep learning it's very tempting to change five things at once because compute is there and you want the number to go up. But when you have to write it down in a table, you notice: wait, this row differs from the baseline in three ways, so what does this result actually mean? That pushes you toward cleaner ablations, one factor at a time, which is how you actually build understanding rather than just chasing a benchmark.

And there's a collaborative side. When I meet with students, I often just ask them to show me the sheet. It's the most honest picture of where the project is. You see the failed runs, the dead ends, the things that surprisingly worked. Papers only show the polished final table, but the spreadsheet is the real research history. Many of the most interesting insights, the "huh, that's weird" moments, come from staring at those rows and noticing a pattern you didn't design for.

So for me, designing the spreadsheet well is almost a proxy for research taste. It reflects whether you know what matters, whether you're being rigorous, and whether you're set up to actually learn something from each experiment rather than just consuming GPUs.

r001.rationale: The response says each row should show what changed and why it was run, and argues for experiments that build understanding rather than merely chase a benchmark. This communicates using tracking to learn from experiments and guide research choices.

r002.rationale: The response criticizes random runs as an uninformative pile of numbers, but does not clearly reject treating accumulated results as evidence that the research is complete.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun question, because people assume the spreadsheet is just bookkeeping, but for me it's actually where a lot of the thinking happens. When you sit down to design the columns, you're forced to decide what you believe matters. Is it the learning rate, the data mixture, the architecture variant, the number of GPUs, the random seed? Every column is a hypothesis about what could explain a difference in results. And once you write it down, you've committed to a space of comparisons. That discipline is good, because it stops you from running experiments that can't be compared to anything.

The other thing is that the spreadsheet makes failure visible. Most experiments don't work. If you just look at your best checkpoint on the leaderboard, you forget that. But when you scroll through two hundred rows and see how many were dead ends, it changes how you reason. You start to notice patterns, like this family of changes always gives a small gain, or this knob never matters no matter how we set it. That's where real intuition comes from, not from the one run that worked.

There's also a social dimension. In a lab with students, the shared sheet becomes the common language. Someone can look at it and immediately ask, why didn't you control for this, or why do these two rows differ in three variables at once. It's a form of peer review that happens before the paper. I actually think a lot of the taste in research is just being very honest in that spreadsheet, including the runs you'd rather not remember.

Of course it has limits. A spreadsheet pushes you toward things that can be measured as a single number, so if the interesting phenomenon is qualitative, like how a model's visual representations change, you have to be careful not to let the table flatten that away. But as a tool for keeping yourself honest, I think it's underrated. Some of my best ideas came from staring at a table and realizing the thing I thought was the story wasn't actually the story.

r001.rationale: The response says spreadsheet columns encode hypotheses, comparable experiments reveal patterns, and those patterns shape research intuition and ideas. This communicates that tracking design makes experiments informative for later research decisions.

r002.rationale: The response notes that many experiments fail and that a best checkpoint can hide those failures, but it does not reject treating accumulated indiscriminate experiments as evidence that research is complete.

astra-6.text:
I think designing that spreadsheet is already part of doing the research. You have to decide: What am I changing? What am I measuring? Which experiments are actually comparable? If you can’t figure out what the columns should be, often that means you haven’t made the research question clear enough yet.

And then the spreadsheet shapes what you pay attention to. If you only record the final accuracy, you’ll naturally optimize for that number. But if you also record compute, training stability, and the hypothesis behind each experiment, you get a much richer picture. A failed experiment can still be useful because you know what it was supposed to test.

So I wouldn’t treat it as just bookkeeping. It’s a way of making your thinking explicit. But you also want to be able to change the spreadsheet—otherwise, the structure you created at the beginning can constrain what you’re able to discover.

r001.rationale: The response says tracking hypotheses and failed experiments makes results informative, but it does not clearly say that each experiment’s information guides the next research decision.

r002.rationale: The response does not address whether accumulating results from indiscriminately run experiments is evidence that research is complete.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it shapes the process more than people realize. When you design that spreadsheet, you’re deciding what matters: what you’re going to measure, which variables you’re going to change, and what makes two experiments comparable. So you’re already putting a structure on your thinking before you run anything.

For example, if you only have a column for accuracy, you’ll naturally focus on accuracy. But if you also track compute, training time, and what hypothesis each experiment is testing, you start asking different questions. Is this improvement worth the cost? Did this result actually support my hypothesis?

The tricky part is leaving room for surprises. A spreadsheet is useful for making experiments systematic, but you don’t want its structure to become the boundary of your research. Sometimes an unexpected result tells you that you need a new column—or a different question altogether.

r001.rationale: The response says spreadsheet design defines what to measure and which hypothesis an experiment tests, then uses results to ask whether a change is worthwhile and whether the hypothesis was supported. This communicates that experiments should inform research decisions.

r002.rationale: The response says spreadsheets should leave room for surprises, but it does not reject treating accumulated results from indiscriminately run experiments as evidence that research is complete.
